title: 16. Greedy Algorithms & Interval Problems
description: Master greedy algorithms and interval problem-solving patterns: Greedy Choice Property and Optimal Substructure, mathematical correctness proofs (Exchange Argument, Greedy Stays Ahead, Induction), Activity Selection and Interval Scheduling (sorting by finish time), Interval Merging (LeetCode 56), Minimum Platforms via two-pointer sweep-line, Fractional Knapsack with value-to-weight ratios, Job Sequencing with Deadlines using Disjoint Set Union (DSU), Huffman Coding lossless compression with Min-Heaps and Prefix Codes, Meeting Rooms I & II, Jump Game I & II (reachability and range expansion), Gas Station circular deficit sweep, CPU Task Scheduler with cooldown periods, and comparative analysis of Greedy vs Dynamic Programming with Coin Change counterexamples.

questions.question: What is the core principle that distinguishes a greedy algorithm from other algorithmic paradigms?
options: It makes the locally optimal choice at each step without reconsidering previous decisions, hoping to achieve a global optimum
It explores all possible branches of a recursion tree before committing to any decision
It caches solutions to overlapping subproblems in a dynamic programming memo table
It divides the problem into two equal halves and recursively solves each half
questions.explanation: A greedy algorithm builds a solution piece by piece by choosing the option that appears best at the current moment without backtracking or reconsidering earlier choices.

questions.question: What does the Greedy Choice Property mean?
options: A globally optimal solution can be assembled by making locally optimal (greedy) choices first without precluding an optimal final outcome
Every choice in the algorithm must consume the minimum possible amount of memory
The problem must be solvable in O(1) time complexity
A choice made at step k can always be undone if a better option appears at step k + 1
questions.explanation: The greedy choice property states that an optimal global solution can be reached by selecting the locally best choice at each step without preventing an optimal outcome.

questions.question: What is the foundational logic of the Exchange Argument in proving greedy algorithm correctness?
options: Show that any hypothetical optimal solution can swap its choice for the greedy choice without decreasing the overall solution quality
Prove that swapping two adjacent array elements always maintains ascending sorted order
Demonstrate that swapping time complexity for auxiliary space complexity is optimal
Exchange recursive calls with iterative loops using an explicit stack
questions.explanation: In an exchange argument, one assumes an arbitrary optimal solution O. If O does not make the greedy choice G, we show that exchanging O's first choice with G results in a new solution O' that is still valid and at least as good as O.

questions.question: In the classic Activity Selection Problem, what is the mathematically proven greedy criterion to maximize non-overlapping activities?
options: Always select the compatible activity with the earliest finishing time
Always select the activity with the earliest starting time
Always select the activity with the shortest duration (finish - start)
Always select the activity with the fewest overlapping conflicts
questions.explanation: Selecting the activity that finishes earliest leaves the maximum remaining time available for subsequent compatible activities. Earliest start or shortest duration can easily produce suboptimal solutions.

questions.question: In LeetCode 56 (Merge Intervals), why must intervals be sorted by their start time before traversal?
options: Sorting by start time ensures intervals are examined chronologically left-to-right, so each interval only needs comparison with the current merged range
Sorting by start time allows binary search to be executed inside each interval
Sorting by start time reduces the space complexity from O(n) to O(1)
Sorting by start time prevents intervals from having negative coordinates
questions.explanation: When sorted by start time, if interval i overlaps with the current merged range (intervals[i][0] <= currentEnd), it is guaranteed to extend or fit within it. Non-overlapping intervals immediately start a new merged range.

questions.question: In the Minimum Number of Platforms problem, what is the two-pointer / sweep-line strategy?
options: Sort arrival times and departure times independently in ascending order, incrementing platforms on arrival and decrementing on departure
Sort train trips by duration and assign platforms using binary search
Use a hash map of train IDs to track platform occupancy
Place all intervals into a disjoint set union data structure
questions.explanation: Since platforms are indistinguishable, we only need to know how many trains are simultaneously at the station. Sorting arrival and departure times separately and traversing with two pointers gives the peak concurrent trains in O(n log n) time.

questions.question: Why does the greedy strategy succeed for Fractional Knapsack but fail for 0/1 Knapsack?
options: In Fractional Knapsack, items can be subdivided so capacity can be completely saturated with highest value-per-weight density without leaving unusable voids
Fractional Knapsack requires fewer than 10 items
0/1 Knapsack values are always floating point numbers
Fractional Knapsack cannot be solved using dynamic programming
questions.explanation: In Fractional Knapsack, taking fractions guarantees that every available kilogram of capacity is filled with the highest possible value per kilogram. In 0/1 Knapsack, taking a high-ratio item might leave empty unusable capacity that could have held two slightly lower-ratio items with a greater total value.

questions.question: In Job Sequencing with Deadlines, what greedy strategy maximizes total profit when all jobs take 1 unit of time?
options: Sort jobs by decreasing profit; schedule each job in the latest available slot at or before its deadline
Sort jobs by increasing deadline; schedule each job in the earliest available slot
Sort jobs by profit-to-deadline ratio and schedule at index 0
Schedule jobs in reverse alphabetical order of job identifier
questions.explanation: To maximize profit, prioritize highest-profit jobs first. Placing a job in the latest possible valid slot preserves earlier slots for jobs with tighter deadlines, maximizing future scheduling flexibility.

questions.question: How does Disjoint Set Union (DSU) optimize the Job Sequencing with Deadlines problem?
options: By allowing parent pointers to point to the latest free slot, finding and updating available slots in near O(1) time via find() and union
By sorting the jobs without calling Arrays.sort()
By calculating the exact factorial of deadlines
By eliminating the need to track job profits
questions.explanation: With DSU, `parent[t]` represents the latest unoccupied slot at or before time `t`. When slot `s` is used, `parent[s] = find(parent, s - 1)`, collapsing chains with path compression so slot lookup takes amortized O(alpha(D)) time instead of O(D).

questions.question: What is a 'Prefix Code' in Huffman Coding, and why is it necessary for lossless data compression?
options: A code in which no character's assigned binary code is a prefix of any other character's code, allowing unambiguous decoding without delimiters
A code where all characters have the exact same bit length (e.g. 8 bits)
A code prefixed with a fixed 32-bit CRC checksum header
A code that orders characters alphabetically by ASCII value
questions.explanation: In a prefix code (or prefix-free code), if character 'A' is '0', no other code can start with '0'. This property allows a bitstream to be uniquely and instantaneously decoded from left to right without ambiguity or separators.

questions.question: How does Huffman Coding construct the optimal prefix tree?
options: Place all characters in a Min-Heap by frequency; repeatedly extract the two lowest-frequency nodes, merge them into a parent node, and reinsert into the heap
Sort characters alphabetically and build a balanced binary search tree
Assign single bits (0 and 1) to the two most frequent characters and discard the rest
Use dynamic programming matrix exponentiation over character frequencies
questions.explanation: Huffman coding repeatedly pairs the two smallest frequency symbols so that they reside at the deepest tree levels (longest codes), while higher frequency symbols remain near the root (shortest codes), minimizing the expected code length.

questions.question: In Meeting Rooms II (minimum rooms required), how is a Min-Heap utilized effectively?
options: The Min-Heap stores the ending times of currently active meetings; if the earliest ending meeting ends <= current start time, reuse that room by polling from the heap
The Min-Heap stores meeting start times in reverse chronological order
The Min-Heap stores the duration of every meeting to prioritize short meetings
The Min-Heap stores room identifiers to balance loads across rooms
questions.explanation: After sorting meetings by start time, the Min-Heap maintains active meeting end times. If `minHeap.peek() <= meeting.start`, that room has been vacated and can be reused (polled and updated with new end time). Otherwise, a new room is allocated. Heap size gives minimum rooms required.

questions.question: In Jump Game I (LeetCode 55), how does the greedy approach verify reachability to the last index in O(n) time and O(1) space?
options: Maintain a variable `farthest = Math.max(farthest, i + nums[i])`; return false if `i > farthest`, and return true if `farthest >= n - 1`
Compute the shortest path using Dijkstra's algorithm on the jump graph
Use backtracking recursion to test all jump lengths from each index
Sort the jump array in descending order and jump from the largest element
questions.explanation: At each index i, if i exceeds the farthest reachable index seen so far, the index is unreachable (return false). Otherwise, update `farthest = Math.max(farthest, i + nums[i])`. If farthest reaches or exceeds the final index, return true.

questions.question: In Jump Game II (LeetCode 45), what do `currentEnd` and `farthest` represent in the greedy range expansion?
options: `currentEnd` is the boundary reachable with the current number of jumps; when i reaches `currentEnd`, another jump is committed and `currentEnd` advances to `farthest`
`currentEnd` is the end of the array; `farthest` is the midpoint of the array
`currentEnd` is the maximum jump value; `farthest` is the array length
`currentEnd` tracks backward jumps; `farthest` tracks forward jumps
questions.explanation: Jump Game II operates like a BFS level traversal: `currentEnd` marks the limit of the current jump level. As i iterates through this window, `farthest` tracks the horizon for the next jump. When i reaches `currentEnd`, we increment jump count and set `currentEnd = farthest`.

questions.question: In the Gas Station Problem (LeetCode 134), why can the starting candidate immediately jump to `i + 1` when the tank becomes negative at station `i`?
options: Because any intermediate station between the starting candidate and i had a positive gas contribution that still could not overcome the deficit at i, so none of them can reach i either
Because station i + 1 is guaranteed to have gas equal to infinity
Because the problem states that every valid start is an even number index
Because all gas stations after i have cost equal to zero
questions.explanation: If starting at station S fails at station i with a negative tank, any intermediate station k (S < k <= i) started with strictly less accumulated fuel than S provided when reaching k. Therefore, k would also fail at or before i. Thus, all stations up to i are eliminated as starting candidates.

questions.question: In the CPU Task Scheduler (LeetCode 621) with cooldown n, what does the formula `(maxFreq - 1) * (n + 1) + countMax` represent?
options: The minimum frame size dictated by the most frequent task types separated by n idle/other slots, plus the trailing group of ties
The total number of CPU clock cycles divided by 26
The maximum cache miss latency of the processor
The sum of all task ASCII values modulo the cooldown
questions.explanation: Tasks with maximum frequency `maxFreq` define `maxFreq - 1` blocks of length `n + 1` (the task followed by n slots). The final block contains just the `countMax` tasks with `maxFreq`. If other tasks overflow these slots, no idle time is needed, yielding `Math.max(tasks.length, requiredTime)`.

questions.question: Consider coin denominations [1, 3, 4] and target amount 6. Why does the greedy choice of picking the largest coin fail to minimize total coins?
options: Greedy picks 4, leaving 2, which requires two 1s (total: 3 coins: 4+1+1), whereas optimal is two 3s (total: 2 coins: 3+3)
Greedy picks two 4s, which exceeds 6 and throws an exception
Greedy sorts coins in ascending order and only picks 1s
Greedy requires all coin denominations to be prime numbers
questions.explanation: For canonical coin systems (like US currency), greedy produces optimal results. But for arbitrary denominations like [1, 3, 4], a locally optimal choice (taking the largest coin 4) prevents finding the globally optimal combination (3 + 3 = 6), proving that general Coin Change requires Dynamic Programming.

questions.question: Which of the following problems requires sorting by finish time rather than start time to apply a greedy choice?
options: Activity Selection / Maximum Non-Overlapping Intervals
Merge Overlapping Intervals
Meeting Rooms I (detecting any conflict)
Meeting Rooms II (allocating minimum physical rooms)
questions.explanation: Activity Selection requires sorting by finish time so that each choice frees up the resource as early as possible. Merge Intervals and Meeting Rooms I/II require sorting by start time to evaluate sequential temporal overlaps.

questions.question: What is a common trap when implementing interval problems with half-open intervals [start, end) vs closed intervals [start, end]?
options: For half-open intervals, meeting A ending at 10 and meeting B starting at 10 do NOT overlap; for closed intervals, sharing time 10 IS an overlap
Half-open intervals can only have integer coordinates, whereas closed intervals accept doubles
Half-open intervals require sorting in descending order
Closed intervals cannot be merged using Arrays.sort
questions.explanation: In half-open intervals `[start, end)`, `end == nextStart` is compatible (no overlap). In closed intervals `[start, end]`, `nextStart <= currentEnd` is an overlap. Mixing these conditions causes off-by-one scheduling bugs.

questions.question: What should an engineer check before committing to a greedy solution instead of dynamic programming in a technical interview?
options: Verify whether the Greedy Choice Property holds, check for counterexamples against the greedy choice, and ensure subproblems remain independent
Check whether the input array is smaller than 100 elements
Check whether the problem can be converted into a binary string
Check whether the company uses Java 8 or Java 21
questions.explanation: The hallmark of rigorous software engineering is validating the Greedy Choice Property: verify that an immediate local choice cannot eliminate an optimal global solution, test against simple counterexamples (like Coin Change), and confirm that optimal substructure applies.
